idiom_name: UnitsNet Length/Mass/... structs + IQuantity runtime surface
implementation_notes: The pattern arrives as a NuGet package rather than hand-written code: UnitsNet generates one immutable struct per quantity (Length, Mass, Duration) with its own unit enum, so Length.FromKilometers(3) + Length.FromMeters(500) performs the conversion in one place and ToUnit(LengthUnit.Millimeter) is the explicit conversion. Since 6.x the value behind a quantity is a fraction-backed QuantityValue with generated exact conversion expressions, which removes accumulated floating-point error from chained conversions, and converting to double is the boundary where that exactness ends; IQuantity, QuantityInfo and UnitParser give the runtime, data-driven view. Hand-writing a readonly struct over a unit enum is still justified for a small closed unit set where the generated API surface (dozens of types, hundreds of properties) is more than the domain needs.
pitfalls: Implicit conversion to double through the Value property (or var inference of QuantityValue) drops the exact rational representation; keep quantities as quantities until a boundary really needs a number.
The generated unit properties are eager conversions: reading Grams instead of Kilograms is a legal, silently wrong expression, so name quantities by the unit they are stored in.
Serialized payloads are affected by the 6.x QuantityValue change; pin an explicit value format for persisted data instead of relying on the default serializer output.

variants.name: Hand-written readonly struct over a unit enum
variants.idiom_name: readonly struct + unit enum + static conversion table
variants.implementation_notes: Without a package, a readonly struct (C# 7.2) over a unit enum with one static conversion table gives the same guarantees for a closed unit set: readonly so it cannot be mutated, IEquatable<T> plus operators so it behaves like a number, private constructors with static factories such as FromMeters so no raw amount can be attached to the wrong unit, and normalisation in the factory so 1000 m and 1 km are the same value. The classic class hierarchy is justified only when units are themselves polymorphic and loaded at run time.
pitfalls: A public constructor or a settable property bypasses the factories and reintroduces the unit-less value the type exists to forbid.
Equality compares the stored amount, so without normalisation to a canonical unit 1000 m and 1 km are unequal and hash differently - normalise in the factory.
Binary floating point drifts over chained conversions; use decimal or a scaled integer for amounts that must round-trip exactly.
